pr_body:
Today any setting under `cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.force.**`
is accepted, but only those matching `...force.*.values` are actually
valid. Accepting other things means that we cannot apply the resulting
cluster state, which is disastrous. This commit adds settings validation
to enforce the expected structure of these settings.

Closes #72524

issue_context.title: Wrong forced shard allocation setting crashing the cluster

**Elasticsearch version** (`bin/elasticsearch --version`):
Version: 7.8.1, Build: default/tar/b5ca9c58fb664ca8bf9e4057fc229b3396bf3a89/2020-07-21T16:40:44.668009Z, JVM: 14.0.1 (and others)

**OS version** (`uname -a` if on a Unix-like system):
Linux server1 4.4.0-1117-aws #131-Ubuntu SMP Tue Oct 6 20:45:33 UTC 2020 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

**Description of the problem including expected versus actual behavior**:
A wrong forced shard allocation awareness setting crashes Elasticsearch, dropping nodes from the cluster and making it no longer possible for them to re-join.

A student by mistake used an underscore (following the attribute name) instead of a dot when configuring forced shard allocation awareness (see https://discuss.elastic.co/t/how-to-completely-reset-forced-shard-allocation-awareness/271710). The bogus setting did not get rejected and brought the cluster state in a non-working configuration. Any bogus setting results in the same behavior.

Expected behavior: A bogus / mal-formatted setting should get rejected.

**Steps to reproduce**:
 1. Start up a cluster
 2. Execute 
```
PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.force.nonsense": ""
  }
}
```

comments: Thanks for the report @dschneiter; I adjusted it slightly to include the cluster applier logs since that's where the problem lies.
By design the force setting takes arbitrary key/values, similar to node attributes. @DaveCTurner Can you elaborate on why you think this is a settings infrastructure issue?

Maybe I'm confused by the meaning of a `groupSetting` but my understanding was that calling `getAsGroups` here is legitimate assuming the setting is valid as a group setting. For instance the `monitor.jvm.gc.collector` group setting behaves similarly: setting `monitor.jvm.gc.collector.nonsense: foo` passes validation and then fails when initialising the `JvmGcMonitorService` for much the same reason:

```

	at org.elasticsearch.node.Node.<init>(Node.java:423) ~[elasticsearch-7.12.0.jar:7.12.0]

	... 6 more
```

(The consequences aren't so severe here since the setting is static and can be fixed).

My reasoning was that the only two group settings I tested had the same issue, so this seemed to be something infrastructural rather than us using the setting wrongly in the decider. It could just be the same bug in both places.

> my understanding was that calling getAsGroups here is legitimate assuming the setting is valid as a group setting

Group settings assume there is a set of arbitrary keys, under which an entire group of settings exist. In this case, instead of the value of the key being a yaml object, it is a direct value. So the settings infrastructure throws an error (though perhaps the error message could be more clear), saying that it expected there to be some subkeys after the user defined key (in your example, the collector name).

So, IMO settings are doing the right thing, throwing an error because the setting is invalid. And we see that in the logs. How that error does not propagate to a failure of the update cluster settings I'm not sure.

In particular:
> The bogus setting did not get rejected and brought the cluster state in a non-working configuration.

Is the setting exception being ignored somewhere and the cluster state still applied?

The `SettingsException` is being thrown _during_ cluster state application, which means we already committed this state so it's too late to do anything about it. We should be detecting that it's invalid before we even start to publish the state.

Now that I look at this again I think I was indeed misunderstanding what these group settings are for, and yes I now think the missing validation is in the allocation code rather than in settings-land itself. I'll relabel this, thanks for your help Ryan.

(and indeed it does seem to be exactly the same bug affecting `monitor.jvm.gc.collector.nonsense`)

review_comments: I am not sure I completely see how applying the state fails when an entry without `values` is found. I do understand it makes little sense though, but depending on how it fails, it may be worthwhile ensure it not only has a `values` entry but also that it is non-empty?

Yes, if you set something of the form `cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.force.attr.not_values` today then that doesn't cause a failure at application time, we simply ignore it, so it's really just another bit of inadvertent lenience in the same area that we should be catching at validation time. The failure only comes from setting something of the form `cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.force.no_more_dots`.

I think an empty `cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.force.attr.values` is valid, it effectively says that the only values of `attr` are the ones that currently exist in the cluster which is the default behaviour if the setting is absent.
Got it now, thanks for the explanation!
